sections.COMMENTS:
This Composite Source is located in the middle of the Po Plain, being one of the outermost and most isolated compressional structures of the Northern Apennines. This structure is a fault-propagation fold related to the Emilia Arc (Northern Apennines thrust system) and deforms the southern part of the Mantova Monocline. This source has been established within the research developed during the European Project GeoMol (http://www.geomol.eu/) based on the study by Maesano and D'Ambrogi (2015).
This study highlighted the recent activity of the thrust related to the Piadena anticline using subsurface geophysical data, and provided the clues to include this fault in DISS as a seismogenic source. This study analyzed the interaction between tectonics and sedimentary processes and provided uplift rates for the last 1.5 Myr, showing that the anticline has been active also during most recent times in the time interval between 450 kyr and the present, although at a reduced rate.
The thrust driving the uplift and the anticline were mapped using the interpretation of a network of seismic lines further constrained by the use of residual Bouguer gravimetric anomalies, which defined the lateral extent of the thrust related anticline.
Altough all these data provided the evidence of the recent activity of the structure expressed by the geometry of growth strata, this is in striking contrast to the lack of historical and instrumental seismicity that could be ascribed to the Piadena Thrust. We suggest that the mismatch between geologic evidence of activity and seismic release may be due either to the incompleteness of the earthquake record for this portion of the plain, at least for its historical part, or to the rather low seismic coupling, or earthquake efficiency of this fault. The last hypothesis would imply that the active deformation is taken up mostly aseismically. We have no clues to solve the problem.
The geometrical parameters of the sources were constrained by the geological sections derived from the interpretation of the available seismic lines by Maesano and D'Ambrogi (2015). Knowing the geometry of the thrust fault, the slip rates of this source were derived from the uplift rates provided in the same work, calculated for several time intervals during the last 1.5 Myrs.
Galli (2005) proposed that the thrust underlying the Piadena anticline may be the source of the 3 January 1117 Veronese earthquake that is perhaps the strongest event occurred in the Po Plain. In his hypothesis the 1117 event was a multiple earthquake, with at least three shocks, one of which badly damaged the nearby town of Cremona.
However, the most updated macroseismic intensity field of this event clearly show that the most damaged area was in the Adige plain south of the town of Verona (Guidoboni et al., 2005). This is considered a clear indication that the seismogenic source of the 1117 earthquake must be located in that area and cannot be elsewhere.
Perhaps because of the widespread effects and the fact that the epicentral area has always been considered an undeformed portion of the foreland, also other investigators located the 1117 event 30-50 km away from the macroseismic epicenter, like along exposed fault systems such as the Veneto thrust front (Galadini et al., 2005).
Conversely, Scardia et al. (2014) based on field evidence and subsurface data suggested that the 1117 earthquake was generated by a NW-SE oriented Mesozoic inherited fault cutting the sedimentary basement, reactivated in the present-day stress regime as a righ-lateral trascurrent fault (the possible source being either the Nogara or the S. Ambrogio fault near Verona). Their seismotectonic model for the central Po Plain area recognizes the main role played by these inherited faults, including short, NNE-directed thrusts belonging to the Giudicarie system segmented by the long, NW-trending reactivated faults.

pictures.t: Location map and geologic cross-section across the Piadena anticline
pictures.c: Location map and geological cross-section across the Piadena anticline showing the deeply buried structure and the thrust detached at the base of the Messinian unconformity. The position of the ramp appears to be controlled by the presence of the inherited normal faults that cut through the Mesozoic limestone deposits and represented an obstacle to the propagation of the flat lying thrust (from Maesano and D'Ambrogi [2015]).

pictures.t: Methodological workflow for unfolding and decompaction
pictures.c: Methodological workflow used for calculating the uplift rates after the unfolding and  decompaction of the deposits folded by the Piadena anticline (from Maesano and D'Ambrogi [2015]).

pictures.t: Topography of Pleistocene unconformities and thickness maps
pictures.c: Topography of the Pleistocene unconformities (A) and thickness maps of the units confined between the different unconformities (B), showing that the Piadena anticline was characterized by a variable local relief through time due to the changing ratio between tectonic and sedimentary rates (from Maesano and D'Ambrogi [2015]).

pictures.t: Vertical separations along strike of the Piadena anticline
pictures.c: Vertical separation through time (A) and along strike (B) of the Piadena anticline, showing that the activity of the structure greatly reduced during the youngest time intervals. The along-strike plot shows the longitudinal full extent of the anticline (from Maesano and D'Ambrogi [2015]).

Comparison between thickness of growth strata and vertical separation across the Piadena anticline through time showing that sedimentation rates have been always greater than the uplift rates, hence the anticline in its history has been mostly blind (from Maesano and D'Ambrogi [2015]).

pictures.t: Structural map of the central-eastern Po Plain
pictures.c: Structural map of the central and eastern Po Plain, showing the different fault systems with different colors. The Mesozoic inherited normal faults that are believed to have controlled the propagation and geometry of Northern Apennines and Southern Alps thrust fronts are shown in blue (from Scardia et al. [2014]).

pictures.t: Seismotectonic model of the central Po Plain
pictures.c: Seismotectonic model of the central Po Plain showing the possible interplay between the Mesozoic inherited normal faults, interpreted to be reactivated in the present-day stress regime as right-lateral strike slip faults, and the thrust fronts of the Southern Alps (from Scardia et al. [2014]).
Geologic map of the Northern Apennines and cross-section showing that the Piadena anticline is a rather isolated and the outermost structure of the thrust belt (from Wilson et al. [2009]).

pictures.t: Seismotectonic sketch of the Po Plain
pictures.c: Seismotectonic sketch of the Po Plain showing historical and instrumental seismicity and the hypothesized association of the Piadena thrust with the 1117 Veronese earthquake (from Galli [2005]).

pictures.t: Regional cross-sections across the Po Plain and the northern Adriatic Sea
pictures.c: Interpreted regional seismic reflection profiles straddling the full extents of the Adriatic basin, including the Po Plain and the adjacent Northern Apennines (to the west), Southern Alps (to the north), and Dinarides (to the east) (from Fantoni and Franciosi [2009]).
